Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?","### Short answer
**It’s not a bug – it’s the new “local‑fonts” mode that MapLibre GL JS uses when the style has no `glyphs` URL.**
When `glyphs` is omitted (or a glyph‑PBF request fails), MapLibre GL JS falls back to **client‑side rendering**:
1. It treats every entry in a layer’s `text-font` array exactly like a CSS `font‑family` list.
2. It asks the browser to resolve that name to a **web‑font** (loaded with `@font-face`) or a **system font** that the OS provides.
3. If the browser can’t find a matching font, it uses its normal CSS fallback chain – which is why you see a “generic” font.
So the map is working as designed
column2: you just haven’t supplied the font that the browser can actually use.

column1: ## What’s really happening under the hood
| Step | What MapLibre does | What the browser does |
| **Style parsing** | Sees no `glyphs` field → enables *local‑fonts mode* (GL JS ≥ 5.11). | – |

| **Layer rendering** | For each `text-font` entry it builds a CSS‑like font‑family string, e.g. `""My Fancy Font"", ""Noto Sans"", sans-serif`. | Calls `document.fonts.load()` (or the native CSS cascade) to resolve the name. |

| **Glyph generation** | If a glyph‑PBF would have been needed, it is **skipped**. Instead MapLibre generates the glyph on‑the‑fly with TinySDF (the same algorithm used for the built‑in CJK fallback). | If the font is available, the browser supplies the glyph outlines
column2: otherwise the fallback font is used. |

column1: ## How to get the exact font you want
### 1. Load the font as a **web font** (the simplest fix)
*Make sure the `font-family` string exactly matches the name you put in `text-font`.*
Now the browser can resolve `""My Fancy Font""` and MapLibre will render the labels with it.
### 2. Serve **glyph‑PBFs** for the font (the classic MapLibre way)

* If the font is one of the common ones (Noto, Open Sans, Roboto, etc.) you can copy the pre‑built PBF tree from a public server (`https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/…`) or from the `openmaptiles/fonts` / `UNDP-Data/fonts` repos.
* For a brand‑new font, generate the PBFs with **Font Maker** or **fontnik**.
2. **Host them** on a domain you control (CORS must allow `*` or your site).
Now MapLibre will request the appropriate `{range}.pbf` files and render exactly the glyph outlines you supplied.

If you *do* want the map to fail loudly when a glyph PBF is missing (e.g., for debugging), you can keep the `glyphs` field but point it at a URL that returns 404 for missing ranges. The map will then log “Unable to load glyph range … Rendering codepoint … locally instead.” and fall back to the generic font – exactly what you’re seeing now. There is no flag to “turn off” the fallback entirely

What's the right way to configure this?,"Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** for getting **offline, local‑font rendering** to work with **MapLibre Native on Android**.
It assumes you are using **MapLibre‑Native ≥ 11.13.0** (the first version that ships the `font-faces` property) and that you do **not** want to run a glyph‑PBF server at all.
| What GL JS does when `glyphs` is omitted | What Native does (today) |

| **No glyph server →** tiny‑SDF generated locally from any web‑font you load (`@font‑face`). | **No automatic fallback** – the style *must* contain a `font-faces` block that tells the native runtime which **local font files** to use for each `text‑font` name **and** which Unicode ranges those files cover. |
| Works out‑of‑the‑box for CJK via `localIdeographFontFamily`. | Same CJK optimisation does **not** exist
column2: you have to supply a local font (or a glyph server) if you want CJK. |

column1: So the **“right way”** on Android is:
1. **Bundle the desired font files** (TTF/OTF) with your APK (or download them once and store them in the app’s private storage).
2. **Add a `font-faces` array** to your style JSON that maps the `text-font` names you use in the style to those bundled files **and** declares the Unicode ranges each file covers.
3. **Reference those `text-font` names** in your layer definitions exactly as you did for a glyph‑PBF stack.
4. (Optional) If you need CJK, add a local CJK font to `font-faces` as well – otherwise you’ll see missing characters.

| **2.1 Choose fonts** | For a global map the safest single‑font choice is **Noto Sans** plus the script‑specific Noto families you need (e.g. `Noto Sans Arabic`, `Noto Sans Devanagari`, `Noto Sans CJK SC`). | Noto covers the vast majority of Unicode and is free. |

| **2.2 Trim to needed ranges (optional)** | If you want to keep the APK small, you can use a tool like **pyftsubset** (from `fonttools`) to create a *subset* that only contains the code‑points you actually display. | Reduces file size dramatically for large CJK fonts. |

| **2.3 Put the files in the app** | Place the `.ttf`/`.otf` files under `src/main/assets/fonts/` (or any folder you like). | MapLibre‑Native can load fonts from the Android assets folder via a `file:` URL. |

| **2.4 Verify the file names** | Keep the file name **exactly** as you will reference it in the style (including extension). Example: `NotoSans-Regular.ttf`. | The `src` field in `font-faces` must be a URL that the native runtime can resolve
column2: using the asset path avoids any ambiguity. |

column1: ## 5. What about CJK and the `localIdeographFontFamily` option?
* **Native does not have a `localIdeographFontFamily` option** (that is a GL‑JS‑only map option).
* If you want CJK characters to render **offline**, you **must** provide a local CJK font via `font-faces`.
* Because CJK blocks contain **tens of thousands of glyphs**, the file can be large (≈ 30 MB for a full Noto CJK SC). If APK size is a concern, consider:
* Subsetting the CJK font to the specific characters you need (e.g. only the city names you ship).

* Shipping the font as a **compressed asset** (`.ttf.gz`) and letting the native runtime decompress it on first use (MapLibre‑Native will read the raw bytes, so you need to unzip yourself before passing the path).
* Using a **fallback to a remote glyph server** only for CJK while keeping other scripts offline – just add a second style source that points at a glyph URL and set `glyphs` to that URL

column1: ## 8. Common pitfalls & how to diagnose them

| **Labels appear as empty boxes (□) or disappear** | The code‑point is not covered by any `unicode-range` in your `font-faces`. | Add a new entry that includes the missing range, or broaden an existing range. |

| **Wrong font is used for a script** | The fallback order in `text-font` picks a font whose range *does* contain the code‑point but whose visual design is not what you expected. | Re‑order `text-font` so the desired script‑specific font appears **before** any generic fallback. |
| **CJK characters are missing** | No CJK `font-faces` entry, or the range is wrong. | Add a CJK entry (or enable a remote glyph server for CJK only). |
| **App crashes on start** | `src` URL is malformed (`file://` missing leading slash) or the file is not packaged. | Verify the exact path: `file:///android_asset/fonts/YourFont.ttf`. |

| **Performance drop when zooming into dense CJK areas** | Large CJK font is being loaded on‑the‑fly for each tile. | Subset the CJK font to only the characters you actually need, or keep the font in memory by pre‑loading it (`Typeface.createFromAsset`). |
You can watch the native logs for messages like:
[MapLibre] FontFace ""Noto Sans Arabic Regular"" loaded from file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf
[MapLibre] Glyph for codepoint U+0627 rendered from local font.
If you see “Unable to load glyph range …” it means the runtime fell back to the **glyph‑PBF** path (which you don’t have). That indicates a missing or mismatched `unicode-range`.

column1: anti-pattern — porting font-faces config from Native to GL JS,skills/maplibre-fonts-glyphs/SKILL.md,I have a working `font-faces` config in my MapLibre Native app's stylesheet that renders local fonts offline with explicit Unicode ranges per file. I'm now building a MapLibre GL JS web app and want the same offline-font behavior — can I copy the same `font-faces` config into my GL JS stylesheet?,"**Short answer:** **No.** The `font‑faces` property is a **MapLibre Native‑only** feature. GL JS does not understand it, and copying the block into a GL JS style will be ignored (or will cause a validation error).
Below is a quick‑reference table, followed by the practical ways you can get the same “offline‑font” experience in a GL JS web app, and the gotchas you should be aware of.
## 1️⃣ Why `font‑faces` won’t work in GL JS
| Feature | MapLibre Native | MapLibre GL JS |

| **`font-faces` property** | Supported (Android ≥ 11.13, iOS ≥ 6.18). You map a `text-font` name → one or more local font files + explicit Unicode ranges. | **Not supported** (see issue [#165](https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-native/issues/165) and GL‑JS issue [#6637](https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-gl-js/issues/6637)). |

| **Glyph‑PBF server (`glyphs` field)** | Optional – you can omit it and rely entirely on `font‑faces`. | Required for the classic SDF pipeline. If omitted, GL JS falls back to **local‑font mode** (see §2) but it is **different** from `font‑faces`. |

| **Automatic local‑font fallback** | Not present (Native still needs a glyph server or `font‑faces`). | Added in GL JS ≥ 5.11.0 – if `glyphs` is missing **or** a particular glyph range fails to load, GL JS will render that range with the browser’s own font‑rendering engine (TinySDF). |
So you cannot simply copy the `font‑faces` JSON block into a GL JS style and expect it to work.
## 2️⃣ How to achieve “offline‑fonts” in GL JS
There are **three** viable approaches, each with different trade‑offs:
| Approach | What you ship | How GL JS finds the glyphs | Offline‑ready? | Rendering consistency (vs Native) |

| **A. Omit `glyphs` and use *local‑font mode*** (GL JS ≥ 5.11) | • Web‑font files (`.woff2`, `.ttf`, etc.) bundled with your site or served from a same‑origin static folder.
• Optional `@font-face` rules or `document.fonts.load()` calls. | GL JS treats every entry in `text-font` as a **CSS‑style font‑family list**. It loads the font via the browser, rasterises each glyph on‑the‑fly with TinySDF, and draws it. | Yes – no external glyph server needed. | **Low to medium**. The exact rasterisation depends on the browser’s font‑rendering engine and on the TinySDF implementation, so the visual result can differ from Native (which uses pre‑computed SDFs). |

| **B. Keep a `glyphs` URL that points to a *self‑hosted* glyph‑PBF tree** | • Pre‑generated `.pbf` files for each font‑stack/range (e.g. from `openmaptiles/fonts`, `UNDP-Data/fonts`, or your own Font‑Maker run).
• A tiny static HTTP server (or CDN) that serves `/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`. | GL JS fetches the PBFs exactly as the style spec describes. | Yes – you just need the static files locally (no external network request if you host them on the same origin). | **High**. The SDFs are identical to what Native would use (provided you use the same font‑stack names). |

| **C. Hybrid: `glyphs` for non‑CJK scripts + local‑font fallback for CJK** | • Glyph‑PBFs for Latin/Arabic/Devanagari/etc.
• No PBFs for CJK (or set `localIdeographFontFamily` to a bundled CJK font). | GL JS loads PBFs for the ranges it has
column2: for missing ranges it falls back to TinySDF (or to the `localIdeographFontFamily` you specify). | Yes – you only need to generate the PBFs you actually care about. | **Medium**. CJK will look like the system font you chose
column3: other scripts will match Native if you use the same PBFs. |

Everything is plain JavaScript (no build tools required) and works with any recent version of **MapLibre GL JS ≥ 2.0** (the hillshade renderer has been stable since v1.13).
MapLibre expects a **raster‑DEM source** that serves **16‑bit elevation tiles** (or 8‑bit if you’re okay with lower precision).
| Provider | URL template | Tile format | Notes |
| **MapLibre demo tiles** | `https://demotiles.maplibre.org/terrain-tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | PNG (16‑bit) | Great for quick prototyping |
| **OpenMapTiles terrain** | `https://tiles.openmaptiles.org/terrain/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | PNG (16‑bit) | Requires an API key for the hosted service |
| **Self‑hosted** | `https://my‑tiles.example.com/terrain/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | PNG or JPEG | Must set `Content‑Type: image/png` (or `image/jpeg`) and enable CORS |

> **Tip:** If you already have a MBTiles file, you can serve it with a tiny static tile server (e.g. `tileserver-gl`, `tileserver-php`, or `tileserver-gl-light`). The only requirement is that the tiles are **single‑band elevation** encoded as 16‑bit PNG (or 8‑bit PNG/JPEG).
## 2. Add the raster‑DEM source to the style
You can either **inject the source into an existing style JSON** or **add it programmatically** after the map is created.
